reason: The sources provide 21 highly consistent, detailed claims from multiple independent sites about the Great Attractor, its hidden nature, and its relationship to the Shapley Supercluster.
story: Did you know our galaxy is being dragged toward an invisible monster? We are hurtling through space at 1.3 million miles per hour, pulled by a mysterious force called the Great Attractor. Located up to 250 million light-years away, this cosmic anomaly is hidden directly behind the Milky Way's thickest band of dust and stars, in a region known as the 'Zone of Avoidance.' For decades, astronomers were blind to what lay there. Using infrared and X-ray telescopes, they finally pierced the veil, discovering the massive Norma galaxy cluster. Yet, Norma's mass isn't nearly enough to explain this terrifying pull. It turns out the Great Attractor itself, along with our entire supercluster of 100,000 galaxies, is being yanked toward an even larger titan: the Shapley Supercluster. We are trapped in a multi-million-light-year cosmic tug-of-war, rushing toward an unseen destination in the dark.
angle: The Milky Way is being dragged through space at 1.3 million miles per hour toward a mysterious mass called the Great Attractor, which is completely hidden from our view behind the Milky Way's own thick dust and stars.

claims.claim: The Milky Way and nearby galaxies are being pulled toward a specific region of space called the Great Attractor.
The Great Attractor is located approximately 150 to 250 million light-years away from the Milky Way.
The Great Attractor lies in the direction of the constellations Norma and Triangulum Australe.
The Great Attractor lies in a region of the sky called the 'Zone of Avoidance,' which is obscured by the gas, dust, and stars of the Milky Way.
Because of interstellar dust and star light, the Great Attractor is difficult to observe at visible (optical) wavelengths.
Astronomers use infrared, radio, or X-ray observations to pierce through the obscuring dust of the Zone of Avoidance.
The Norma Cluster (Abell 3627) is a massive galaxy cluster located within the Great Attractor region.
The Norma Cluster lies approximately 220 million light-years away from the Milky Way.
Evidence of large-scale, non-uniform galaxy motion in the direction of the Great Attractor first emerged during the 1970s.
In the 1980s, a collaboration of astronomers nicknamed the 'Seven Samurai' identified the Great Attractor.
The Seven Samurai mapped this movement by studying the distances and velocities of over 400 elliptical galaxies.
Astronomer Alan Dressler coined the name 'Great Attractor' for this mass concentration.
In 2014, the Great Attractor was defined as the central basin of attraction for a newly mapped supercluster of galaxies named Laniakea.
The Laniakea Supercluster is a massive structure that spans approximately 500 million light-years.
Laniakea contains around 100,000 galaxies, including the Milky Way.
The boundaries of Laniakea are defined by mapping the 'peculiar velocity' of galaxies, which is their motion independent of cosmic expansion.
The mass of the Great Attractor region alone is insufficient to explain the full gravitational pull acting on local galaxies.
The Great Attractor and nearby structures are themselves being pulled toward an even larger mass concentration called the Shapley Supercluster.
The Milky Way is traveling through space toward this region at a speed of around 1.3 million miles per hour (or 2.2 million kilometers per hour).
Measurements of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) showing a dipole pattern provided early proof of our galaxy's motion relative to the cosmic rest frame.
Astronomer Brent Tully and his colleagues led the 2014 mapping project that defined the boundaries of the Laniakea Supercluster.

disputed: The exact mass of the Great Attractor: Early models estimated it at 10^16 solar masses (S1), but later X-ray surveys showed the Norma region is less massive (S1, S4), with much of the pull coming from the more distant Shapley Supercluster. The script should explain that initial mass estimates were revised downward as astronomers mapped more distant structures.

Whether the Milky Way will actually reach the Great Attractor: S6 notes that the Milky Way will likely never arrive at the Great Attractor because cosmic expansion (driven by dark energy) will pull it away, while S1 notes the Great Attractor itself is moving toward the Shapley concentration rather than being a final endpoint. The script should handle this by explaining that the Great Attractor is not our final destination, as cosmic expansion and the pull of the Shapley Supercluster will prevent us from ever falling into it.

The physical size of Laniakea: S1 and S5 state it spans approximately 500 million light-years, while S7 claims it is more than 520 million light-years across. The script should state 'around 500 million light-years' or reference '500 to 520 million light-years' as the estimated span.
